What happens to a Montana tenant when the landlord sells?

A sale does not cancel the lease. The buyer becomes the landlord. Under Montana Code Annotated 70-26-102, whoever receives property that carries reserved rent gets the seller's remedies for unpaid rent, broken lease terms, waste or forfeiture.

So a tenant cannot be pushed out just because a sale is coming. A buyer who wants a vacant house must wait for the lease to run out or use a lawful termination route, and a buyer who wants an investment can keep the tenant and the rent.

The seller gets protection too. Under 70-24-304, a landlord who conveys the premises in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act for events after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance. Unless otherwise agreed, the seller stays liable for all security recoverable by the tenant and for all prepaid rent.

Practically, give the tenant written notice of the sale and settle the deposit and prepaid rent with the buyer at closing, so the money follows the lease.

Montana laws that govern a rental

Most residential rentals fall under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act of 1977, MCA Title 70, chapter 24, and the Residential Tenants' Security Deposits chapter, Title 70, chapter 25. The Montana courts website points landlords and tenants to those two laws, plus chapter 26 on landlord and tenant residential and commercial matters and the state's prohibited discriminatory practices statute in Title 49.

Chapter 25 applies to all rentals of dwellings subject to Title 70, chapter 24, or chapter 33, which covers mobile home lots. Federal fair housing law applies on top of the state rules.

Laws behind a Montana residential rental
LawSubject
MCA Title 70, chapter 24Residential Landlord and Tenant Act of 1977
MCA Title 70, chapter 25Residential tenants' security deposits
MCA Title 70, chapter 26Landlord and tenant, residential and commercial
MCA Title 49, chapter 2, part 3Prohibited discriminatory practices
42 U.S. Code, chapter 45Federal fair housing

The Montana Judicial Branch hosts a landlord handbook of 31 pages and a tenant handbook of 29 pages, along with forms, on its landlord and tenant page. Both sides can read them without paying anything.

Notice required to end a Montana tenancy

How long the notice must be turns on why the tenancy is ending. Under 70-24-441 a month-to-month tenancy ends on at least 30 days' written notice from either side, and a week-to-week tenancy needs 7 days. When the tenant breaches, 70-24-422 sets shorter periods that vary by the breach.

  • Unpaid rent: 3 days to pay after written notice of the missed rent and the landlord's intent to terminate.
  • Unauthorized pet: 3 days.
  • Unauthorized people living in the unit: 3 days.
  • Most other violations: 14 days, and the lease continues if the tenant fixes the problem before the date in the notice.
  • Same breach repeated within 6 months: at least 5 days' written notice.
  • Verbal abuse of the landlord, or damage or danger to the premises or neighbors: 3 days.

Choosing the 30-day month-to-month notice frees the landlord from the breach rules in 70-24-422. Under 70-24-423, taking the full rent owed wipes out a claimed breach only if that breach was nonpayment.

Put the notice in writing and describe the acts or omissions. If a sale hinges on getting possession, follow the statute word for word.

How a Montana landlord evicts, and where the forms are

A tenant who stays past a valid notice can be taken to court by the landlord in an action for possession. The courts site has a Notice to Vacate, an Action for Possession packet, a Writ of Assistance form, and a letter telling a tenant about extra cleaning charges after move-out.

Section 70-24-427 gives a landlord a claim for possession, rent and damages once the rental agreement has ended. Under 70-24-422(5), a landlord may recover actual damages and seek an injunction for a tenant's noncompliance, and may recover treble damages if the noncompliance is purposeful, though not for early termination of the tenancy.

Retaliation is not allowed. Section 70-24-431 bars a landlord from raising rent, cutting services or threatening a possession action because a tenant complained to a housing-code agency, complained in writing about a violation, or joined a tenant organization. A landlord who tries to clear a house for a sale right after a repair complaint should expect that issue to come up.

Free help is available. The Court Help Program, at (406) 841-2975, offers free assistance on common civil legal issues, and the Montana Legal Services HelpLine is 1-800-666-6899.

Deposit and entry rules while a sale is pending

A landlord may show the house, but entry limits still bind. At least 24 hours' notice is required, unless there is an emergency or notice is impracticable, and entry must come at reasonable times. Book the photographer, appraiser or inspector with that lead time in mind.

Deposit rules matter just as much. Section 70-25-102 applies chapter 25 to covered dwellings, and 70-25-206 calls for a statement of the premises' condition when the lease starts. When the tenancy ends, the landlord has 30 days to deliver a written list of charges and any balance, or 10 days if nothing is owed. A landlord who misses the list forfeits the right to withhold for damage or cleaning.

  • Put the deposit amount and the tenant's move-in condition statement in the sale file.
  • Let the purchase contract say whether the deposit moves to the buyer or is credited at closing.
  • Keep a copy of the written notice of the sale that you send the tenant.

Does a tenant change how a rental sells for cash?

Yes. Occupancy, the rent and the lease end date shape what a buyer will pay. Offers treat a tenant-occupied house either as an income property or as a future vacant one.

A cash buyer can take the house with the tenant still there, so you need not rush a move-out or fund repairs before closing. To hand over an empty house, use the notice periods above. A month-to-month tenancy needs the full 30 days.

Property tax can help explain the numbers to a buyer. A home leased to tenants as their residence, for stays of 28 or more days and at least seven months of the year, qualifies for the Long-Term Rental Reduced Rate. Vacation rentals and second homes pay the flat 1.90% rate for 2026, so how a buyer uses the house changes the tax bill.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Montana landlord end a lease early because the house is being sold?

Not on that ground alone. The buyer inherits the existing lease, so the tenant remains until it ends or a lawful termination applies. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended by either side with 30 days' written notice under MCA 70-24-441.

How many days does a Montana tenant have to pay rent after a notice?

Three days, counted from written notice of the missed rent and of the landlord's intent to terminate. Miss that window and the landlord may terminate, and the tenant must leave under MCA 70-24-422.

Who keeps the security deposit when a Montana rental sells?

The selling landlord stays liable to the tenant for security recoverable under Title 70, chapter 25, and for prepaid rent, unless otherwise agreed. Sellers normally work this out with the buyer at closing.

How much notice must a Montana landlord give before entering a rental?

A full day, meaning 24 hours' notice, except in an emergency or when giving notice is impracticable. MCA 70-24-312 also limits entry to reasonable times.

Where can a Montana landlord find eviction forms?

The state courts' landlord and tenant page has a Notice to Vacate, an Action for Possession packet, a Writ of Assistance form and a landlord handbook.

How probate works in Montana

Montana has adopted the Uniform Probate Code, which gives an estate two paths, informal and formal. Probate is the court-supervised cleanup after a death: collecting and looking after property, paying what is owed, and handing the remainder to those who inherit.

One person, the personal representative, carries it out; some call that role administrator or executor. Estate size and the presence of a valid will decide which path fits, and the Montana courts site has a questionnaire that suggests one.

Before an inherited house can be sold, somebody has to hold legal authority to sign the deed. In an informal appointment the clerk handles the application. Under MCA 72-3-225, the clerk may make the appointment effective after 120 hours of elapsed time from the death, and only after the findings required by 72-3-222.

StageRule and statute
Start the caseInformal or formal case, usually opened inside 3 years of death (72-3-122)
AppointmentClerk may act after 120 hours from death (72-3-225)
Creditor noticeNewspaper notice weekly for 3 weeks, then 4 months for claims (72-3-801)
Close the estateSworn statement no earlier than 6 months after appointment (72-3-1004)

Deadline to open a probate

As a general rule, a probate or appointment case cannot be opened once 3 years have gone by since the death (MCA 72-3-122). Exceptions exist, so an old inherited house is not automatically stuck.

A late informal appointment or formal proceeding is still possible when no one filed anything on the succession during those 3 years. The trade-off is narrow powers: the representative may hold estate assets only as far as needed to confirm title in the successors, and no claims except administration expenses can be brought against the estate. A will contest can be filed within the later of 12 months from the informal probate or 3 years from the death.

Moving early makes sense for a house left empty after a death. Without someone in authority it cannot be sold, yet property tax, insurance and wear keep adding up.

Who can sign the deed on an inherited house?

Under MCA 72-3-613, a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate property, land included, by public or private sale, unless the will or a court order says otherwise. The title company will want proof of that authority before closing.

Family can keep living in the house while the estate is open. Section 72-3-606 lets the representative leave real property with, or hand it to, the person presumed entitled to it, unless possession is needed to administer the estate. That same section makes the representative responsible for paying taxes and for reasonable steps to manage, protect and preserve estate assets.

  • Will in place: the executor it names applies for appointment and follows its terms.
  • No will: heirs under the intestacy statutes apply, and the court or clerk makes the appointment.
  • Joint tenant or recorded beneficiary deed: the house may skip probate entirely. A transfer on death deed form, tied to MCA 72-6-415, is linked from the courts site.
  • Joint tenancy or a life estate: Montana State University Extension publishes a guide to transferring such property without probate.

Creditor claims and how the estate closes

Once appointed, the representative runs a notice in a county newspaper, one issue a week for three weeks. It announces the appointment, gives an address, and warns creditors that claims presented later than 4 months after first publication are forever barred (MCA 72-3-801). Creditors the representative knows about may also get a mailed notice, which gives them the later of 4 months from publication or 30 days from the mailing.

A second cutoff sits in 72-3-803: claims not presented by the earlier of 1 year after death or the date in the notice are barred. Between the two rules, heirs and buyers can see when the debts settle.

Section 72-3-1004 covers closing by sworn statement. The representative files it no sooner than 6 months after the original appointment, and it must confirm the claims period is over, that claims, expenses and taxes are paid or arranged, and that distributees and known creditors received a copy. One year after the statement is filed, the appointment ends if no proceeding involving the representative is pending.

A sale does not have to wait for closing. Proceeds generally pass through the estate, so ask the attorney, or read the court file, to find out who gets the net money and when.

Cash sale of an inherited house

With a cash buyer the closing moves fast. Funds arrive without a mortgage lender, the personal representative signs the deed on the strength of the letters of appointment, and the title company files it with the county. Nothing needs fixing, emptying or staging beforehand.

Delays usually come from a will not yet admitted, heirs who disagree, a house left vacant in winter, or overdue taxes. Property tax does not pause for probate: one half falls due November 30, the other May 31, and paying late adds interest plus a 2% penalty (MCA 15-16-102).

Gather these before you take any offer:

  • A death certificate, any will, and the letters of appointment.
  • What the county treasurer shows as owed in tax.
  • Names and phone numbers for every heir, so each can sign off on the price.
  • Photos and a short repair list, so an offer matches how the house really looks.

With the paperwork in order, the buyer's title company matches the representative's authority to the deed, looks for recorded liens, and records the sale. No lender appraisal or loan approval is involved, and those are the steps that most often stall an estate sale.

Cash Home Buyers will write an offer on an inherited Montana house and fit it around the court's schedule. Treat this page as general information and not legal advice. For your own case, ask a probate attorney or the clerk of court.

Free and low-cost probate help

The Montana courts point families to several places. Call the Court Help Program at (406) 841-2975 for free help with common civil legal issues, probate among them. The Legal Service Developer Program, part of the Department of Public Health and Human Services, answers at 1-800-332-2272. For low-income Montanans with urgent civil legal problems, Montana Legal Services Association staffs a HelpLine at 1-800-666-6899 on weekdays from 9:00 am to 1:00 pm. The State Bar of Montana has a lawyer referral service at (406) 449-6577.

The courts site also offers an affidavit of death, a small estate packet, and an affidavit for collection of personal property packet. For a small estate, one of those packets may save you a full court case.

Frequently asked questions

How long do I have to start a probate in Montana?

Usually 3 years after the death (MCA 72-3-122). A late case is possible if nothing was filed in that time, though the representative's rights over estate assets are then limited.

Can I sell a house in Montana before probate is finished?

Yes, once a personal representative is appointed, unless the will or a court order restricts sales (MCA 72-3-613). Before that, nobody has clear authority to sign.

How long do creditors have to file claims against a Montana estate?

Four months from first publication of the notice, or 30 days from a mailed notice when that ends later. Section 72-3-803 also bars claims 1 year after death if that comes first.

Does the house have to stay with the personal representative during probate?

No. MCA 72-3-606 allows leaving it with the person presumed entitled to it, unless the representative needs possession to administer the estate.

When can a Montana personal representative close the estate?

With a verified statement filed no sooner than 6 months after the original appointment, once the claims period is over and the estate is administered (MCA 72-3-1004).
